title: Given a monolithic (e.g. food-delivery) application, how would you decompose it into microservices (DDD bounded contexts, database-per-service, extract one module at a time), and what challenges do you face?
keyPoints: Start by finding bounded contexts using DDD, not by cutting code along technical layers.
Decompose by business capability (Payments, Loans, Accounts) so each service owns a coherent domain.
Use the Strangler Fig pattern: route one capability at a time to a new service, never a big-bang rewrite.
Splitting the shared database is the hardest part: replace joins with API calls or event-driven read models.
Local transactions become Sagas with compensating actions and eventual consistency.
Extract the module with fewest dependencies first for an early, low-risk win.
Decompose only where teams genuinely need independent deployment; be willing to merge back if a boundary fails.

s1_definition.oneliner: Decompose along DDD bounded contexts, give each service a private database, extract one module at a time with the Strangler Fig, and expect the hard parts to be the shared database and the shift from local transactions to sagas.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Bounded contexts** – use Domain-Driven Design to identify areas with their own language and rules; each becomes a candidate service.
- **Business capability** – decompose by what the business does (Payments, Loans) not by technical layer (Controllers, DAOs).
- **Strangler Fig** – extract one capability at a time while the monolith keeps running; never a big-bang rewrite.
- **Database split** – give each service its own database; replace cross-service joins with API calls or event-driven read models.
- **Transactions** – local ACID transactions become Sagas with compensating actions and eventual consistency.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India as one huge building where accounts, payments, loans, and notifications all share the same giant ledger room. Decomposing it is like moving each department into its own building with its own ledger, one department at a time, while the bank stays open the whole time. You start by drawing clear department boundaries (bounded contexts), give each its own books (database-per-service), and move the easiest, least-connected department first.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When decomposing a monolith, start by finding boundaries using Domain-Driven Design, not by cutting code. At National Bank of India, I identify bounded contexts like Account, Payment, Loan, and Notification, and decompose by business capability rather than by technical layer. I never do a big-bang rewrite: I use the Strangler Fig pattern to extract one module at a time while the monolith keeps running.

The hardest challenge is always the shared database. When Payment moves out, it gets its own database and can no longer join the accounts table. I replace that join with an API call or a local read model kept fresh by events. Local transactions become Sagas with compensating actions, trading strong ACID for eventual consistency.

The senior-level point is restraint. I extract the module with the fewest dependencies first for an early win. I decompose only where teams genuinely need independent deployment or scaling. And I am willing to merge a service back if the boundary turns out to create coordination without autonomy.

Remember one sentence: decompose along DDD bounded contexts, extract one module at a time with the Strangler Fig, give each service a private database, and expect the hard parts to be splitting the shared database and replacing local transactions with Sagas.
